paper_metadata.title: Prognosis of Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy with eye-closure sensitivity

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the setting and inclusion criteria. However, it uses a convenience sample from a tertiary center, which may introduce selection bias as these patients often have more severe or refractory epilepsy compared to the general JME population.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (ECS) was measured using a highly rigorous Video-EEG Neuropsychological Protocol (VNPP), which is superior to standard EEG or clinical interview alone. This reduces misclassification bias significantly.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Eye closure sensitivity (ECS) is a unique EEG phenomenon described as the non-incidental appearance of transient epileptic abnormalities following the closure of the eyes for 1–4s during a standard EEG recording
items.reasoning: The study provides a precise electro-clinical definition of the prognostic factor.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: all patients had a 4–6 h video-EEG monitoring... using a digital equipment... in addition to perioral and deltoid electrodes, besides palpebral electrodes
items.reasoning: The use of palpebral electrodes and a standardized 4-6 hour video-EEG protocol ensures high reliability.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: We defined three types of EM: a) flicker... b) flutter... and c) jerk
items.reasoning: The study uses established clinical categories for the prognostic factor.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Our VNPP was based on those reported by Matsuoka et al. [29] and Guaranha et al. [30].
items.reasoning: A standardized protocol was applied to all participants in the same clinical setting.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Group 1 included 22 JME patients with ECS and EM confirmed by VNPP.
items.reasoning: The PF was the basis for group assignment; all analyzed patients had confirmed PF status.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Outcomes were measured using seizure diaries, which are standard in epilepsy research but rely on patient recall and self-reporting, introducing potential subjective bias. However, the long follow-up and use of 'seizure days per month' help stabilize this data.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: The frequency of seizures was assessed using a diary... Myoclonia and absence frequencies were quantified as seizure days per month
items.reasoning: The outcomes (seizure frequency and freedom) are clearly defined and quantified.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: The frequency of seizures was monitored by standard seizure calendars.
items.reasoning: Seizure calendars are standard but prone to patient reporting bias; no objective confirmation (like ambulatory EEG) was used for the long-term outcome.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All patients were followed-up... Seizure types and precipitant factors, AEDs therapy, and treatment adherence were observed.
items.reasoning: The follow-up and recording methods were consistent across both groups.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study accounts for several confounders (psychiatric comorbidities, AED load, photosensitivity) and shows the groups were homogeneous at baseline for many factors. However, it does not use multivariable regression to adjust for the significant baseline difference in 'age of onset', which could independently influence prognosis.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Psychiatric comorbidity was also analyzed... For the comparative evaluation of AEDs administered, the concept of AED load was applied
items.reasoning: Key confounders like treatment intensity (AED load) and psychiatric status were measured.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: AED load... was calculated by summing the ratios between the prescribed dose and the World Health Organization defined doses
items.reasoning: The study uses the WHO-defined daily dose for a standardized measure of treatment.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Psychiatric comorbidity was also analyzed through Schedule Clinical Interview for DSM-IV, Axis I (ICD-10), and/or 'The Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview' (MINI)
items.reasoning: Validated psychiatric instruments (MINI, STAI) were used.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Groups were homogeneous with respect to... neuropsychological findings
items.reasoning: The assessment protocol was identical for both groups.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Groups were homogeneous with respect to gender, age, duration of epilepsy...
items.reasoning: The study attempted to compare similar groups, but they were not matched, and age of onset differed significantly.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Comparison between Groups 1 and 2 was performed by the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test... Fisher's exact test
items.reasoning: The analysis relies on univariable tests (Mann-Whitney, Fisher's) and lacks multivariable adjustment for confounders like age of onset.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical analysis is straightforward and appropriate for the sample size, but the lack of multivariable modeling limits the ability to isolate the effect of ECS from other variables. Reporting is transparent regarding the differences found.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Comparison between Groups 1 and 2 was performed by the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test for quantitative variables. The Fisher's exact test was applied for qualitative variables.
items.reasoning: The statistical methods are clearly stated.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No multivariable model was built; the study only performed group comparisons.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
items.reasoning: Univariable tests are adequate for descriptive comparison but insufficient for definitive prognostic modeling in the presence of confounders.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Results: Group 1 had a lower age at epilepsy onset (p = 0.028)... Psychiatric comorbidities were not different between groups.
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings across all measured domains.
